title: Blog 1
content:
Web Tier Auto Scales Smoothly — Why Does It Still Spin Under 10,000 Users? Dissecting the Database Bottleneck and Combining Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) with Amazon RDS Read Replicas
When first learning Cloud, it is easy to adopt a confident assumption: put an Application Load Balancer in front, enable an Auto Scaling Group for EC2, and the web application can handle any volume of traffic.
I used to think the same—until running a load stress test for my project. When simulated concurrent traffic jumped from a few hundred to 10,000 concurrent users:
The Auto Scaling Group scaled exactly as configured: 2 EC2 → 4 EC2 → 8 EC2. CPU utilization across the web server fleet hovered comfortably around 40–50%. Yet in the browser, the homepage took 6–8 seconds to load before eventually throwing timeout errors. Checking Amazon CloudWatch revealed that the bottleneck was not the EC2 tier at all: the backing Amazon RDS instance was pegged at 100% CPU.
1. Why Does EC2 Auto Scaling Unintentionally “Choke” the Database? A typical real-world website (e-commerce, news portal, community forum) exhibits a heavily skewed access ratio: roughly 80–90% READ operations (browsing product lists, reading articles, checking carts) and only 10–20% WRITE operations.
When traffic spikes:
The more EC2 instances the Auto Scaling Group spins up, the more SELECT queries hit the exact same single RDS instance simultaneously. Thousands of concurrent requests repeatedly fetch identical hot data (for example, top 10 flash-sale items or leaderboards). The database must constantly read from EBS storage, burning through IOPS and CPU cycles on redundant queries, which in turn slows down critical write transactions such as order creation and checkout payments. In short: A stateless Web tier scales horizontally with ease, whereas a single stateful Database becomes the sole performance bottleneck of the entire architecture.
2. First Line of Defense: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) & the Cache-Aside Strategy Before upgrading RDS to a costly larger instance class, the first question to ask is: which data changes infrequently yet gets read the most?
Instead of forcing RDS to recompute the exact same query 10,000 times per minute, I placed Amazon ElastiCache for Redis inside the Private Subnet directly in front of the Database using the Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) pattern:
Cache Hit: When an EC2 instance needs the featured product list, the application checks Redis first. If present in RAM, Redis responds in typically under 1 millisecond. RDS never even sees the request. Cache Miss: If the key is absent from Redis (or its TTL has expired), EC2 queries RDS, returns the result to the user, and populates Redis with an appropriate TTL (e.g., 60 seconds or 5 minutes). Invalidation: Whenever data is updated in the DB (e.g., a product price change), the application should delete (or update) the corresponding key in Redis so the next read fetches fresh data. Relying solely on TTL means users may see stale data until expiration. In my lab benchmark, offloading roughly 80% of repetitive queries to the Redis layer cut RDS CPU utilization nearly in half. Exact gains depend heavily on query complexity and cache hit ratio, so always benchmark on your own workload.
3. Second Line of Defense: Amazon RDS Read Replicas — Divide and Conquer Reads What about complex read queries (search, dynamic filtering, analytics reports) that cannot all be cached in Redis? This is where Amazon RDS Read Replicas step in.
AWS lets you create one or more read-only copies of a Primary DB using asynchronous replication. At the application layer, I cleanly separated two connection paths:
Primary Endpoint: Handles write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and reads requiring strict immediate consistency. Read Replica Endpoint: Absorbs heavy analytical and catalog SELECT workloads. Important Note: With standard RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL, each Read Replica exposes its own individual endpoint rather than a single auto-load-balanced “reader endpoint”. If you provision multiple replicas, your application must distribute connections across endpoints—or use Route 53 weighted records pointing to the replicas. Built-in reader endpoints are provided by Amazon Aurora (and RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters).
By offloading read traffic, the Primary DB stays dedicated to safe, low-latency writes, while read throughput scales horizontally simply by adding Read Replicas.
4. Four Practical “Traps” Students Commonly Hit During Implementation While building the lab and reading AWS operational guides closely, I learned that adding caching and replicas isn’t plug-and-play. Watch out for these 4 common pitfalls:
Trap 1: Confusing Multi-AZ Standby with Read Replicas. Many beginners assume enabling Multi-AZ gives them an extra DB node to serve reads. For a standard Multi-AZ DB instance, the standby exists purely for High Availability via synchronous replication—applications cannot route read queries to it. To scale reads, you must provision a Read Replica. (Note: Multi-AZ DB clusters do offer readable standbys, which is a separate architecture option.) Trap 2: Replication Lag. Because Read Replicas replicate asynchronously, there is always a slight delay behind the Primary—from tens of milliseconds up to several seconds under peak load. If a user clicks “Place Order” (writing to Primary) and the confirmation page immediately runs a SELECT against a Read Replica, it may throw “Order not found”. Always route read-after-write flows straight to the Primary endpoint. Trap 3: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd on TTL Expiration). If thousands of keys expire at the exact same timestamp (such as midnight 00:00), thousands of requests simultaneously suffer a cache miss and slam RDS at once. A simple fix is adding TTL jitter (e.g., 300s + random(0..30s)) to stagger expirations. For ultra-hot keys (such as top flash-sale items), jitter alone isn’t enough—you should add request coalescing/locking (allowing only one request to repopulate the cache) or proactive refresh before expiration. Trap 4: Memory Eviction and Costs in ap-southeast-1. If you push every query into ElastiCache without sensible TTLs or memory limits, Redis fills up RAM and triggers eviction of older keys, degrading your cache hit ratio. Cost-wise, in the Singapore region (ap-southeast-1), a small cache.t4g.micro node costs around ~$13/month (730 hours) based on pricing checked during my lab (always verify current AWS pricing pages). That is affordable for student project testing, but spinning up 2–3 large Read Replicas and forgetting to delete them afterward will spike your month-end bill quickly. 5. Key Architectural Takeaways After evolving the architecture from a basic Web Scale setup into a Read-Optimized Architecture, three golden rules stood out:
Do not rush to scale up the DB instance before inspecting your Read/Write ratio. Most database saturation in typical web apps stems from redundant reads rather than write CPU limits. Follow the read-optimization hierarchy: Intercept hot data in RAM (ElastiCache Redis) → offload complex analytical reads to RDS Read Replicas → upgrade instance class only as a last resort. Always clean up lab resources: Delete Read Replicas and ElastiCache clusters immediately after benchmarking to keep Free Tier / AWS Credits safe. One extra tip: As EC2 instance counts grow, total concurrent DB connections increase proportionally and can become a bottleneck of their own. When that happens, look into connection pooling or Amazon RDS Proxy.
References (AWS Official Documentation) Amazon RDS Read Replicas Overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html Amazon ElastiCache Caching Strategies (Cache-Aside): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html Amazon RDS Multi-AZ vs. Read Replicas: https://aws.amazon.com/rds/features/read-replicas/ Amazon ElastiCache Pricing (ap-southeast-1): https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/pricing/ Best Practices for Amazon RDS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_BestPractices.html Original Blog Link on AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19pPm2zNwx/

title: Blog 2
content:
S3 and EC2 Are in the Same Region — Why Does My NAT Gateway Bill Keep Climbing? Uncovering the Private Subnet Internal Data Transfer Cost Trap and Fixing It 100% Free with VPC Gateway Endpoint
When learning standard AWS network architecture, the very first security rule we apply is placing all application servers (EC2, ECS) inside a Private Subnet so no Public IPs are exposed to the Internet, and placing a NAT Gateway in the Public Subnet so internal servers can still download packages or call external APIs.
I built that exact textbook architecture for a data processing project:
The backend running on EC2 (Private Subnet) compressed logs, generated daily reports, and pushed backup archives to Amazon S3, while reading/writing state records in Amazon DynamoDB—all located within the exact same Singapore (ap-southeast-1) region.
Everything ran smoothly and securely. Yet opening Billing & Cost Management at the end of the month delivered an unexpected surprise: beyond the fixed hourly NAT Gateway charge, the NAT Gateway Data Processing line item climbed by dozens of dollars even though the application barely called any external APIs.
The culprit was a routing detail I had overlooked when first studying VPCs: by default, Amazon S3 and DynamoDB reside outside your VPC and use Public IP ranges—meaning every byte traveling between EC2 and S3 was silently “detouring” through the NAT Gateway.
1. Why Is Internal AWS Traffic Billed Through the NAT Gateway? When an EC2 instance inside a Private Subnet executes aws s3 cp or writes to S3 via an AWS SDK:
The hostname s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com resolves to an AWS Public IP address. EC2 checks the Private Route Table attached to its subnet. Because there is no explicit internal route defined for S3, packets match the final catch-all rule: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx (NAT Gateway). Hundreds of gigabytes of backup files or datasets traverse the NAT Gateway (and Internet Gateway) just to reach S3. In the Singapore region (ap-southeast-1), NAT Gateway charges on two separate dimensions:
Fixed Hourly Fee: $0.059/hour (roughly $43.07/month over 730 hours, even with zero traffic). Data Processing Fee: $0.059/GB of data passing through. Even a modest workload pushing/pulling 500 GB/month with S3 (application logs, user media, database dumps) adds $29.50/month in NAT Gateway data processing charges—even though the data never needed to leave AWS’s regional network.
2. The Zero-Cost Solution: How Does a VPC Gateway Endpoint Work? To keep all S3 and DynamoDB traffic strictly inside AWS’s internal backbone (AWS Private Backbone) without touching a NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway, AWS provides VPC Gateway Endpoints.
It works via Longest Prefix Match routing prioritization in your Route Table:
You create a VPC Gateway Endpoint (vpce-xxxx) targeting Amazon S3 (or DynamoDB) and associate it with your Private Route Table. AWS automatically injects a route entry referencing an AWS Managed Prefix List (pl-s3-id, representing all S3 public IP ranges in that region) pointing directly to vpce-xxxx. From that point onward:
Packets destined for S3/DynamoDB match pl-s3-id → vpce-xxxx (more specific than 0.0.0.0/0) and flow directly over the AWS internal network at $0/hour and $0/GB. Software package updates (apt update) or calls to third-party public APIs continue routing cleanly via 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx. 3. Routing Architecture Upper Branch (Matched Prefix List): Traffic from EC2 to S3 and DynamoDB within the same region is steered by the Private Route Table through the VPC Gateway Endpoint over AWS’s private backbone ($0/GB). Lower Branch (Default Route 0.0.0.0/0): Only outbound Internet traffic or requests targeting S3/DynamoDB in a different region pass through the NAT Gateway in the Public Subnet ($0.059/hour + $0.059/GB). (Note: The diagram is simplified and omits the Internet Gateway sitting between the NAT Gateway and the Internet). 4. Four Technical “Traps” Easily Hit During Configuration Trap 1: Confusing Gateway Endpoints (Free) with Interface Endpoints (Hourly Billed). Currently, only Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB support completely free Gateway Endpoints. Other AWS services (SQS, SNS, Secrets Manager, ECR, CloudWatch, etc.) require Interface Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) billed per AZ (~$0.01/hour/AZ plus data processing fees). S3 supports both Gateway and Interface types—accidentally selecting Interface for S3 will still incur hourly charges. Trap 2: Creating the Endpoint but Forgetting to Select the Private Route Table. If you omit selecting the Private Subnet’s Route Table during Gateway Endpoint creation, AWS cannot insert the pl-s3-id → vpce-xxxx route. The Endpoint sits idle while traffic quietly keeps flowing through the NAT Gateway. Trap 3: Cross-Region S3 Bypasses the Gateway Endpoint (and Triggers Double Charges). VPC Gateway Endpoints only operate within the same Region (e.g., EC2 in ap-southeast-1 accessing a bucket in ap-southeast-1). If your bucket resides in us-east-1, its IP range isn’t covered by Singapore’s Prefix List, forcing traffic back through the NAT Gateway ($0.059/GB) plus Inter-Region Data Transfer fees. Trap 4: Locking Yourself Out of Console, CLI, and SDK When Enforcing aws:SourceVpce in Bucket Policies. A major security perk of Gateway Endpoints is adding an explicit Deny rule in your S3 Bucket Policy blocking any access not originating from your specific vpce-xxxx (using StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpce). However, applying this rule without an exception blocks all external access—including AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, and local SDK calls (Access Denied). Always include an exception clause (such as ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalArn) for your admin IAM Role or IAM User. 5. How to Verify It Works in 30 Seconds Check the Route Table: Go to VPC → Route Tables → select your Private Route Table → Routes tab, and confirm a route exists with Destination pl-xxxxxxxx (com.amazonaws.ap-southeast-1.s3) and Target vpce-xxxxxxxx. Check NAT Gateway CloudWatch Metrics: Upload a 1–2 GB test file from EC2 to S3. Inspect the BytesOutToDestination metric on the NAT Gateway—the graph remains flat at 0 instead of spiking. 3-Line Summary EC2 instances in a Private Subnet transferring large S3 payloads without a Gateway Endpoint incur NAT Gateway data processing fees on top of hourly charges. Enable a VPC Gateway Endpoint ($0/GB, $0/hour) to keep same-region S3 and DynamoDB traffic inside AWS’s private backbone. Always associate the correct Private Route Table, keep buckets in the same region, and carve out an aws:PrincipalArn exception when restricting Bucket Policies with aws:SourceVpce. In your own projects, do you automatically enable VPC Gateway Endpoints for S3/DynamoDB from day one when placing servers in a Private Subnet, or did a surprise NAT Gateway bill catch you first? Feel free to share your experience!
References Gateway VPC Endpoints: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpce-gateway.html Gateway Endpoints for Amazon S3: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html Amazon VPC & NAT Gateway Pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/ AWS PrivateLink Pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/privatelink/pricing/ AWS Managed Prefix Lists: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/.../managed-prefix-lists.html Original Blog Link on AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/154F8Gp26wY/

title: Proposal
content:
SMART KITCHEN SMART KITCHEN PLATFORM A proposal to develop a platform that supports food discovery, home cooking, and finding nearby ingredient suppliers.
Information Details Project source code repository https://github.com/veexto/AWS-Final-Project-Cooking/tree/main Deployed website https://d18x1ou8x7botm.cloudfront.net/ AWS Region Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 Date November 2026 1. Background and Motivation 1.1. Project Background In modern life, choosing meals, finding cooking recipes, and preparing ingredients are common needs. However, information about dishes, cooking instructions, and ingredient suppliers is often scattered across multiple platforms. Users may spend time finding meals that match the ingredients they have, their budget, and their shopping options.
Smart Kitchen is a web platform that helps users discover dishes, explore home-cooking recipes, and find ingredient suppliers based on their current location or a manually entered address. The project uses AWS services to deploy the frontend, process requests, store data, connect to location search services, and integrate AI capabilities through Amazon Bedrock.
1.2. Motivation and Objectives Simplify food discovery and help users choose recipes that match their needs. Provide ingredient information and cooking instructions to support home cooking. Help users find nearby ingredient suppliers based on their current location or a provided address. Build an AWS-hosted web application with an architecture that can be maintained and scaled. Integrate Amazon Bedrock to add generative AI request-processing capabilities to the application. 1.3. Expected Outcomes A website accessible through its AWS deployment URL. Users can browse, search, and filter the recipe data available in the system. Users can view dish ingredients and cooking instructions. The system can receive location search requests and return results from Amazon Location Service. The system can send requests to Amazon Bedrock and receive responses from the integrated AI model. The user interface, server-side processing, database, and AI services are connected through AWS services. 2. Solution Architecture 2.1. Architecture Overview Smart Kitchen uses a serverless web architecture on AWS. Frontend files and static assets are stored in Amazon S3, while Amazon CloudFront is configured as the content delivery layer in front of S3. When users access the website through the CloudFront domain, CloudFront receives the requests, serves content from the S3 origin, and can cache content at edge locations to improve page-loading performance. Business requests generated by user interactions are sent directly from the frontend to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS, then forwarded to AWS Lambda for processing. Lambda retrieves recipe data from Amazon DynamoDB, calls Amazon Location Service when location searches are required, or calls Amazon Bedrock when AI functionality is needed.
Amazon Bedrock is integrated into the server-side processing flow. AWS Lambda acts as an intermediary that receives requests, sends prompts to the AI model, and processes the responses before returning results to the user interface. This approach keeps service credentials and access permissions on the server side instead of exposing them in frontend source code.
2.2. AWS Architecture Diagram 2.3. AWS Services and Their Roles AWS Service Role in the Project Amazon S3 Stores the website’s frontend files and static assets. Amazon CloudFront Acts as the content delivery network (CDN) in front of Amazon S3, receives website access requests, serves frontend files from S3, and helps accelerate content delivery through caching at edge locations. Users access the website through the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. Amazon API Gateway Provides API endpoints for communication between the user interface and server-side processing. AWS Lambda Receives and processes business logic, retrieves data, and orchestrates calls to AWS services. Amazon DynamoDB Stores and retrieves cooking recipe data. Amazon Location Service Supports location/store searches based on a user’s location or entered address. Amazon Bedrock Provides access to generative AI models; the project integrates Amazon Nova Micro to process AI requests from the application. 2.4. Main Application Workflows Website access: Users open the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. CloudFront receives the request and serves frontend files from S3; content can be cached at edge locations to reduce loading time when requested again. Recipe discovery: The user interface sends a request to API Gateway; Lambda processes the request and retrieves recipe data from DynamoDB before returning the results. Location search: Users provide their GPS location or enter an address; Lambda calls Amazon Location Service and returns the results to the user interface. AI request processing: The user interface sends a request to API Gateway; Lambda receives and validates the input, then calls Amazon Bedrock with the Amazon Nova Micro model. Lambda receives the model response, processes the result, and returns it to the user interface. 2.5. Scalability and Reliability Using AWS-managed and serverless services reduces the need to manage servers and allows individual components to scale according to demand. Amazon S3 stores the frontend, while CloudFront distributes content from S3 to users and supports edge caching. API Gateway and Lambda handle the application’s business requests, and DynamoDB provides the data storage layer. Amazon Location Service and Amazon Bedrock are invoked when the application needs location search or AI processing capabilities.
Monitoring, alerting, backup, and performance optimization mechanisms will be considered according to operational needs and budget. For Amazon Bedrock, request volume, service quotas, and response times must be monitored to minimize any negative impact on the user experience.
3. Security Design 3.1. Identity and Access Management Apply the principle of least privilege and grant each component only the permissions it requires. Use IAM roles for Lambda when accessing DynamoDB, Amazon Location Service, and Amazon Bedrock. Grant only the permissions required to invoke Bedrock models, such as the InvokeModel action for the model being used. Do not place access keys, secret keys, or credentials in frontend source code or public repositories. Separate AWS resource administration permissions from the application’s execution permissions. 3.2. Data and API Protection Prefer HTTPS for connections between users and the website/API; users access the website through the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. Validate and verify input data before processing. Do not expose sensitive information, credentials, or internal implementation details in API responses. Configure CORS, authentication, and request rate limits according to the application’s actual requirements. Control the content sent to Amazon Bedrock and avoid sending unnecessary personal or sensitive data. Process and validate AI model responses before returning results to the user interface. 3.3. Monitoring and Logging Amazon CloudWatch can be used to monitor logs, errors, and metrics from Lambda and related AWS components. For the Bedrock integration workflow, model invocation errors, response times, and quota usage should be monitored. Log retention periods, alert configurations, and monitoring levels will be adjusted according to operational needs and budget. Credentials and sensitive user data must not be written to logs.
4. Project Scope and Deliverables 4.1. Project Scope A. Food and Recipe Discovery Display a list of cooking recipes. Support searching and discovering dishes based on the designed criteria. Display ingredient information and cooking instructions. Provide recipe data for users to reference when cooking at home. B. Finding Nearby Ingredient Suppliers Allow users to provide their current location by granting GPS permission or manually entering an address. Send location search requests to the server-side processing layer. Use Amazon Location Service to find relevant places and return the results to the user interface. C. AI Integration with Amazon Bedrock Integrate Amazon Bedrock into server-side processing to handle AI requests from the application. Use the Amazon Nova Micro model through the server-side processing workflow. Receive requests from the user interface, send them to the AI model, and return responses to the user interface. Handle errors that occur during model invocation and service responses. 4.2. Future Development Scope Expand personalized recommendations based on users’ ingredients, budgets, preferences, and needs. Improve the integration of recipe data and AI responses to help users plan meals. Expand food-service discovery capabilities and connections with restaurants/businesses. 4.3. Out of Scope Full online payment processing. Inventory management and real-time stock synchronization. Delivery services or real-time order tracking. Comprehensive management of restaurant business operations. Large-scale data analytics. 4.4. Project Deliverables The Smart Kitchen website deployed on AWS. A user interface stored in Amazon S3 and distributed through Amazon CloudFront. A backend/API using API Gateway and AWS Lambda. A recipe database in Amazon DynamoDB. A location search feature integrated with Amazon Location Service. An AI feature integrated with Amazon Bedrock using the Amazon Nova Micro model. Project proposal documentation and an overall architecture diagram. 5. Implementation Roadmap The project is divided into major phases. The schedule may be adjusted according to actual progress and team resources.
Phase Main Activities Deliverables Phase 1: Planning Identify the problem, objectives, requirements, and project scope. Project requirements and plan. Phase 2: Application Development Build the user interface, server-side processing, and core features. User interface and server-side processing. Phase 3: AWS Infrastructure and Data Set up S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. Deployed and connected application components. Phase 4: External Service and AI Integration Integrate Amazon Location Service and Amazon Bedrock; configure the required access permissions, connect the Amazon Nova Micro model to server-side processing, and test the response workflow. Location search and AI features integrated into the application. Phase 5: Documentation and Handover Complete project documentation, architecture, cost estimation, and Workshop materials. Project documentation package. Start and end dates will be added according to the actual implementation schedule; weekly activity records are presented in the Worklog section.
6. AWS Cost Estimation 6.1. Estimation Basis and Assumptions Costs are estimated for approximately 100–500 active users per month, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 region. This represents a small-to-medium operating scenario using a serverless architecture and includes only the services currently present in the Smart Kitchen architecture.
The assumptions used for the estimate are:
Approximately 100–500 active users per month. Approximately 20,000–100,000 requests to API Gateway per month. Approximately 1,000–5,000 location search requests through Amazon Location Service per month. Amazon Bedrock usage is estimated at 50 calls per user per month, equivalent to 5,000 calls for 100 users and 25,000 calls for 500 users. Each call uses an average of 1,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. Frontend files, images, and recipe data require relatively little storage; no continuously running EC2 instances are used. CloudFront traffic is estimated at 20 GB and 20,000 HTTPS requests per month for the 100-user scenario, and 100 GB and 100,000 HTTPS requests per month for the 500-user scenario. The table records the AWS Pricing Calculator results before considering any eligible offers or free usage allowances. 6.2. Estimated Costs by User Scale The following table summarizes the estimated costs from the AWS Pricing Calculator for scenarios with 100 and 500 active users per month. All prices are calculated for the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 region, in USD/month.
AWS Service 100 users/month (USD) 500 users/month (USD) Amazon S3 0.04 0.18 Amazon CloudFront 2.42 12.12 Amazon API Gateway (REST API) 0.09 0.43 AWS Lambda 0.01 0.05 Amazon DynamoDB 0.01 0.05 Amazon Bedrock (Nova Micro) 0.71 3.53 Amazon Location Service 0.55 2.75 Amazon CloudWatch 0.07 0.37 Estimated total/month 3.90 19.48 According to the current AWS Pricing Calculator results, the estimated cost is USD 3.90/month for 100 users and USD 19.48/month for 500 users. These are estimates based on assumed usage, not actual invoices.
Calculation details:
Amazon S3: 1 GB/5 GB of storage; 500/2,500 Tier 1 requests; 20,000/100,000 Tier 2 requests. Amazon CloudFront: 20 GB/100 GB of data transfer out to the Internet; 20,000/100,000 HTTPS requests. Amazon API Gateway: 20,000/100,000 REST API requests. AWS Lambda: 625/3,125 GB-seconds, assuming 128 MB of memory and an average execution time of 1 second. Amazon DynamoDB: 10,000/50,000 read request units and 10,000/50,000 write request units. Amazon Bedrock: 5,000/25,000 units of 1,000 input tokens and 2,500/12,500 units of 1,000 output tokens; assuming 50 calls per user per month, with 1,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens per call. Amazon Location Service: 100/500 Geocode requests and 1,000/5,000 SearchNearby requests. Amazon CloudWatch: 0.1/0.5 GB of log ingestion and 0.1/0.5 GB-Mo of log storage. The CloudFront costs in the table reflect the amounts currently displayed by the Calculator for the entered usage levels. When determining the actual budget, the account’s pricing plan, Free Tier/offer eligibility, and applicable free allowances must be checked. These amounts should not be assumed to be free until eligibility has been verified.
6.3. Factors That May Affect Costs Amazon Location Service: Number of store/place searches and the type of data requested in each request. Amazon Bedrock: Number of Nova Micro model calls and the input/output token volume of each request. Amazon CloudFront: Amount of distributed data and number of HTTPS requests; the Calculator results should be checked against the AWS account’s pricing plan and eligible free allowances. API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB: Number of requests, execution time, data volume, and query patterns. Amazon S3 and CloudWatch: Storage volume, number of read/write operations, and log retention period. 6.4. Cost Control and Optimization Measures Review AWS Billing regularly and configure budget alerts. Avoid repeated Amazon Location Service calls when users have not changed their location or search criteria. Control the number of Amazon Bedrock calls, prompt length, and response token count. Optimize CloudFront caching for static frontend files. Optimize DynamoDB queries and Lambda execution time. Periodically compare estimates with actual costs and adjust the budget based on system usage. This estimate is intended to illustrate the potential operating costs when the application serves 100–500 users per month. Once actual operating data is available, the assumptions in the AWS Pricing Calculator should be updated to produce a more accurate estimate for the system’s usage.
7. Project Management, Risks, and Conclusion 7.1. Project Team and Responsibilities Member Role Responsibilities Huỳnh Minh Hiệp Frontend Developer & UI/UX Designer Design and develop the website interface; build food search and filtering features, display recipes, and connect the frontend to the backend. title: Blog 3
content:
Re-running Last Week’s Pipeline Gives Totally Different Numbers: Code Change or Overwritten S3 File? Combining Amazon S3 Versioning and SHA-256 Checksums to Achieve Data Reproducibility for Data Processing Pipelines
When building a data processing pipeline or ML training project on AWS, almost everyone starts with a clean-looking storage layout like this:
A daily ETL Ingestion pipeline overwrites the latest dataset at a single fixed Amazon S3 path, e.g., s3://data-lake-bucket/clean/dataset.csv. Downstream, AWS Lambda or EC2 reads that exact path to compile reports or train models. Everything runs smoothly until the day you need to audit or reproduce last week’s metrics:
You re-run the exact same commit of last week’s code against s3://data-lake-bucket/clean/dataset.csv. The generated output deviates completely from the submitted report. At that moment, nobody knows whether the discrepancy comes from a recent code edit or whether dataset.csv on S3 was silently overwritten by yesterday morning’s ETL run. Without a mechanism to freeze input dataset versions, every testing, debugging, or audit task turns into pure “guesswork”.
1. Why Shouldn’t You Use S3’s ETag to Verify File Integrity? When first exploring how to detect whether an S3 object changed, many engineers (myself included) immediately think of the ETag field returned by the S3 API. However, that is a classic trap:
S3 only returns an ETag equal to the file’s MD5 checksum when uploaded via a single-part upload using default SSE-S3 encryption. As soon as a file grows large enough for the SDK to automatically trigger Multipart Upload, or when the bucket uses AWS KMS encryption (SSE-KMS), the ETag is no longer the MD5 hash of the full file (for Multipart Uploads, ETag is the MD5 of the concatenated part MD5s followed by a part-count suffix, such as "...-5"). Consequently, comparing a locally computed MD5 hash against S3’s ETag causes false integrity mismatches even when the file is completely intact. Instead of relying on ETag, the robust approach is using SHA-256 (S3 natively supports ChecksumAlgorithm='SHA256' on upload, or you can compute it directly in application code) paired with S3 Versioning.
2. Combining S3 Versioning + a SHA-256 Manifest To guarantee that any historical pipeline run can reproduce 100% of its exact input data, the system relies on three building blocks:
Enable S3 Versioning on the data bucket: Every time ETL overwrites clean/dataset.csv, S3 preserves older data and automatically assigns the new upload a unique VersionId (e.g., v1, v2). Older records transition into Noncurrent Versions and are completely immutable—nobody can alter the bytes inside an existing VersionId. Record a Manifest in Amazon DynamoDB: Whenever a pipeline starts a run (Run ID), the application writes a Manifest record capturing: Bucket, Key, the exact VersionId read, and its SHA-256 digest. Read by pinned VersionId and verify SHA-256 before processing: When re-running an older job for auditing, the pipeline does not read the default key path (which always points to the latest v2). Instead, it fetches the Manifest from DynamoDB, invokes GetObject with VersionId=v1, recomputes the SHA-256 hash over the downloaded byte stream, and compares it against the Manifest. Only on an exact match does processing proceed; if the hash mismatches or the version is missing, the pipeline aborts immediately (Fail Fast) instead of emitting corrupted reports. 3. Pipeline Data Reproducibility Architecture ETL Ingestion: Continuously overwrites new files onto Amazon S3. With Versioning enabled, the prior version v1 remains preserved alongside the new v2. Step 1 (Manifest DB): The Pipeline Runner writes or reads pinned metadata (VersionId + SHA-256 hash) in Amazon DynamoDB. Step 2 (GetObjectVersion): The Pipeline Runner fetches the exact pinned dataset version (v1) from S3 rather than accidentally reading the latest version (v2). Step 3 (Integrity Check): Compares the computed SHA-256 digest against the Manifest. On match, the pipeline runs; on mismatch, it aborts immediately (Fail Fast) to protect output accuracy. Automated Cleanup: An S3 Lifecycle Rule periodically expires aged noncurrent versions (NoncurrentVersionExpiration) to keep storage costs under control. 4. Four Technical “Traps” Easily Hit During Implementation Trap 1: Granting s3:GetObject but forgetting s3:GetObjectVersion. In IAM Policies, s3:GetObject only grants read access to the Current Version. As soon as your code passes a VersionId parameter to reproduce older data, AWS rejects the request with AccessDenied unless the IAM Role also includes s3:GetObjectVersion. Trap 2: S3 bills quietly inflating because Noncurrent Versions are never cleaned up. In Singapore (ap-southeast-1), every noncurrent version in S3 Standard is billed full storage rates ($0.025/GB/month for the first 50 TB). If a 10 GB dataset is overwritten daily across 30 days, you are billed for 300 GB ($7.50/month instead of $0.25/month)—even though the default S3 Console view (with Show versions toggled off) only displays 1 file. Always configure an S3 Lifecycle Rule to transition old versions to cheaper tiers (NoncurrentVersionTransition) or expire them after a retention window (NoncurrentVersionExpiration). Trap 3: Assuming a standard delete frees up storage space. On a versioned bucket, calling DeleteObject without specifying a VersionId does not remove actual bytes—it simply inserts a Delete Marker on top. All underlying noncurrent versions stay on disk and keep accruing monthly charges until you explicitly delete each VersionId. Trap 4: Trusting ETag for Multipart Uploads or SSE-KMS encrypted objects. As covered in Section 1, always store and verify checksums using SHA-256 (via S3’s built-in ChecksumSHA256 support or streaming application hashing) rather than treating ETag as an integrity signature. 5. How to Verify in 30 Seconds Check in the S3 Console: Open your bucket → toggle “Show versions” at the top of the object list → confirm that every overwrite creates a distinct Version ID entry instead of erasing prior versions. Test the Fail-Fast guard: Manually alter one character in the SHA-256 string stored inside the DynamoDB Manifest item and trigger a pipeline re-run → the runner must immediately refuse execution and raise a data integrity mismatch error. 3-Line Summary Never rely solely on a mutable S3 path if you need to reproduce historical pipeline runs reliably. Enable S3 Versioning paired with a Manifest storing VersionId + SHA-256 checksums (instead of ETag) to lock down input dataset versions. Grant s3:GetObjectVersion in IAM and configure an S3 Lifecycle Rule early so noncurrent versions do not bloat your monthly storage bill. In your data engineering or AI/ML projects, do you version S3 datasets via date-partitioned folders (e.g., dt=2026-11-26/) or by enabling S3 Versioning? Feel free to share your approach!
References Using Versioning in S3 Buckets: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html Checking Object Integrity in Amazon S3 (SHA-256): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity.html Managing Noncurrent Versions with S3 Lifecycle: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-configuration-examples.html Amazon S3 Pricing (ap-southeast-1): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/ Original Blog Link on AWS Study Group: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/151HogtQqMT/

title: Deploy AWS Lambda Backend
content:
1. Create the Lambda Function Navigate to AWS Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch. Configure the basic parameters: Function name: RecipeSearchFunction Runtime: Python 3.12 Execution role: Select Use an existing role → RecipesLambdaRole. Go to Configuration → General configuration → Edit, and increase Timeout to 15 seconds. Go to Configuration → Environment variables, and add 2 environment variables: DYNAMODB_TABLE: RecipesTable BEDROCK_MODEL_ID: apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0 2. Architecture & Functional Breakdown of lambda_function.py The lambda_function.py source code is divided into 6 main functional blocks, handling the entire pipeline from receiving HTTP requests, validating inputs, and connecting to 3 core AWS services (DynamoDB, Amazon Location Service, Amazon Bedrock) to returning standardized JSON responses to the frontend.
2.1. Configuration Initialization & AWS SDK Clients import base64 import json import logging import math import os import random import unicodedata import urllib.error import urllib.request from decimal import Decimal from urllib.parse import parse_qs, quote import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1") BEDROCK_REGION = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_REGION", REGION).strip() TABLE_NAME = os.environ.get("DYNAMODB_TABLE", "RecipesTable").strip() BEDROCK_MODEL_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_MODEL_ID", "apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0").strip() BEDROCK_API_KEY = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_API_KEY", "").strip() MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 200 MAX_KEYWORDS = 10 dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name=REGION) table = dynamodb.Table(TABLE_NAME) geo_places_client = boto3.client("geo-places", region_name=REGION) bedrock_client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=BEDROCK_REGION) CORS_HEADERS = { "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type,Authorization", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET,POST,OPTIONS", "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8", } Key Functions: Reads environment variables (AWS_REGION, BEDROCK_REGION, DYNAMODB_TABLE, BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, BEDROCK_API_KEY) to decouple configuration from source code, enabling easy updates without code changes. Pre-initializes SDK connections (boto3.resource / boto3.client) in the global scope: table (DynamoDB), geo_places_client (Location Service Places v2), and bedrock_client (Bedrock Runtime). Placing them outside lambda_handler allows connection reuse across Warm Start invocations, reducing response latency. Configures CORS_HEADERS so browsers accessing from the CloudFront domain can invoke API endpoints (GET, POST, OPTIONS) without being blocked by browser security policies. 2.2. Utilities, Normalization & Input Security def json_default(value): if isinstance(value, Decimal): return int(value) if value % 1 == 0 else float(value) raise TypeError(f"Unsupported JSON value: {type(value).__name__}") def response(status_code, body): return { "statusCode": status_code, "headers": CORS_HEADERS, "body": json.dumps(body, ensure_ascii=False, default=json_default), } json_default() & response(): Converts DynamoDB Decimal numeric types into standard JSON int/float and wraps HTTP responses with status codes (200, 400, 500) and CORS headers. def normalize(value): text = str(value or "").strip().lower() text = text.replace("đ", "d") text = unicodedata.normalize("NFD", text) return "".join(ch for ch in text if unicodedata.category(ch) != "Mn") normalize(): Normalizes Vietnamese strings into lowercase without diacritics (converting đ -> d and decomposing Unicode accents via NFD) so ingredient and mood keyword matching remains accurate even when users omit accent marks. def csv_values(value, field_name): if not value: return [] if len(value) > MAX_INPUT_LENGTH: raise ValueError(f"Tham số {field_name} vượt quá {MAX_INPUT_LENGTH} ký tự.") values = [part.strip() for part in value.split(",") if part.strip()] if any(len(part) > 60 for part in values): raise ValueError(f"Mỗi giá trị trong {field_name} tối đa 60 ký tự.") return [v for v in values[:MAX_KEYWORDS] if not any(c in v for c in "<>{}$`\\;")] csv_values(): Enforces maximum input length (MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 200), caps keywords at 10 (MAX_KEYWORDS = 10), and strips dangerous special characters (<>{}$\\;`) to prevent injection attacks. def query_params(event): params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {} if params: return params raw = event.get("rawQueryString", "") return {k: v[0] for k, v in parse_qs(raw).items() if v} def parse_json_body(event): body = event.get("body") or "{}" if event.get("isBase64Encoded"): body = base64.b64decode(body).decode("utf-8") try: return json.loads(body) except (TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError): raise ValueError("Dữ liệu gửi lên không phải JSON hợp lệ.") query_params() & parse_json_body(): Standardizes parameter parsing across both API Gateway REST API v1 and HTTP API v2 event formats (including Base64 decoding when applicable). 2.3. Query & Filter Recipes (Amazon DynamoDB) def get_all_recipes(): items = [] kwargs = {} while True: result = table.scan(**kwargs) items.extend(result.get("Items", [])) last_key = result.get("LastEvaluatedKey") if not last_key: break kwargs = {"ExclusiveStartKey": last_key} items.sort(key=lambda x: str(x.get("RecipeID", ""))) logger.info("Loaded %s recipes from %s", len(items), TABLE_NAME) return items get_all_recipes(): Scans all items from RecipesTable (automatically handling LastEvaluatedKey pagination for larger datasets) and sorts them by RecipeID. def matches(recipe, filters): ingredients = recipe.get("Ingredients") or [] allergens = recipe.get("Allergens") or [] nutrition = recipe.get("Nutrition") or {} if filters["ingredients"] and not has_any(ingredients, filters["ingredients"]): return False if filters["health"] and not has_tag(recipe, "HealthTags", filters["health"]): return False if filters["need"] and not ( has_tag(recipe, "HealthTags", filters["need"]) or has_tag(recipe, "DietTags", filters["need"]) ): return False if filters["mood"] and not has_tag(recipe, "MoodTags", filters["mood"]): return False if filters["allergies"] and ( has_any(ingredients, filters["allergies"]) or has_any(allergens, filters["allergies"]) ): return False if filters["avoid"] and has_any(ingredients, filters["avoid"]): return False numeric_rules = ( ("maxTime", "CookingTimeMinutes"), ("maxBudget", "EstimatedCostVND"), ) for param, field in numeric_rules: if filters[param] is not None: try: value = float(recipe.get(field)) except (TypeError, ValueError): return False if value > filters[param]: return False for param, field in (("maxSodium", "SodiumMg"), ("maxCarbs", "CarbsG")): if filters[param] is not None: try: value = float(nutrition[field]) except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError): return False if value > filters[param]: return False return True matches(): Applies multi-criteria filtering to each recipe: available ingredients (ingredients), allergens (allergies), excluded ingredients (avoid), dietary/health preferences (health, need), mood (mood), and numeric thresholds (maxTime, maxBudget, maxSodium, Empathetic AI Chef Chatbot (Amazon Bedrock) def find_recipes_by_mood_weather(msg, items): norm_msg = normalize(msg) # 1. Ưu tiên cao nhất: Khớp trực tiếp tên món ăn (chính xác hoặc gần đúng) exact_name_matches = [] partial_name_matches = [] for r in items: r_name = normalize(r.get("Name", "")) if not r_name: continue if r_name == norm_msg or r_name in norm_msg: exact_name_matches.append(r) elif len(norm_msg) >= 4 and norm_msg in r_name: partial_name_matches.append(r) if exact_name_matches: # Ưu tiên tên món dài hơn (khớp chi tiết hơn) lên đầu, không shuffle exact_name_matches.sort(key=lambda r: len(normalize(r.get("Name", ""))), reverse=True) return exact_name_matches, True if partial_name_matches: partial_name_matches.sort(key=lambda r: len(normalize(r.get("Name", "")))) return partial_name_matches, True # 2. Ưu tiên thứ hai: Khớp theo nguyên liệu xuất hiện trong câu nhắn (xếp theo số nguyên liệu khớp) ing_scored = [] for r in items: ings = [normalize(ing) for ing in (r.get("Ingredients") or []) if normalize(ing)] matched_ings = [ing for ing in ings if ing in norm_msg] if matched_ings: # Ưu tiên món khớp nhiều nguyên liệu hơn ing_scored.append((len(matched_ings), r)) if ing_scored: ing_scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) top_count = ing_scored[0][0] top_ing_recipes = [r for cnt, r in ing_scored if cnt == top_count] random.shuffle(top_ing_recipes) rest_ing_recipes = [r for cnt, r in ing_scored if cnt < top_count] return top_ing_recipes + rest_ing_recipes, False # 3. Ưu tiên thứ ba: Khớp theo tâm trạng / thời tiết / chế độ ăn target_moods = [] target_cats = [] if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["mua", "lanh", "se lanh", "buon", "stress", "ap luc", "am bung", "co don"]): target_moods.append("comforting") target_cats.extend(["soup", "main"]) if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["nong", "oi buc", "nang", "ngan", "nhe bung", "giam can", "thanh dam", "mat"]): target_moods.extend(["fresh", "light"]) target_cats.extend(["salad", "side", "soup"]) if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["met", "duoi", "ue oai", "can nang luong", "doi", "tap gym", "vui"]): target_moods.append("energizing") target_cats.append("main") scored = [] for r in items: score = 0 r_moods = r.get("MoodTags") or [] if any(m in r_moods for m in target_moods): score += 2 if r.get("Category") in target_cats: score += 1 if ("chay" in norm_msg or "thanh dam" in norm_msg) and "vegetarian" in (r.get("DietTags") or []): score += 3 if score > 0: scored.append((score, r)) scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) if not scored: return [], False top_score = scored[0][0] top_group = [r for score, r in scored if score >= max(1, top_score - 1)] random.shuffle(top_group) rest_group = [r for score, r in scored if score < max(1, top_score - 1)] return top_group + rest_group, False find_recipes_by_mood_weather(): Analyzes the semantics of the user’s message (e.g., cold rain, sad, stressed, hot weather, tired) to map them to MoodTags (comforting, fresh, light, energizing) and corresponding dish categories, while excluding previously suggested dishes (excludeIds) to prevent repetition. def handle_chat(event): payload = parse_json_body(event) user_message = str(payload.get("message") or "").strip() if not user_message: raise ValueError("Vui lòng nhập tâm trạng, thời tiết hoặc câu hỏi của bạn.") if len(user_message) > 500: raise ValueError("Câu hỏi tối đa 500 ký tự.") items = get_all_recipes() shuffled_items = list(items) random.shuffle(shuffled_items) exclude_ids = set(payload.get("excludeIds") or []) matched_recipes, is_explicit_dish = find_recipes_by_mood_weather(user_message, items) if is_explicit_dish: candidate_recipes = matched_recipes else: fresh_matches = [r for r in matched_recipes if r.get("RecipeID") not in exclude_ids] candidate_recipes = fresh_matches if fresh_matches else matched_recipes suggested_id = candidate_recipes[0].get("RecipeID") if candidate_recipes else None suggested_name = candidate_recipes[0].get("Name") if candidate_recipes else None menu_context = "\n".join([ f"- [{r.get('RecipeID')}] {r.get('Name')}: loại {r.get('Category')}, " f"tâm trạng phù hợp: {', '.join(r.get('MoodTags') or [])}, " f"chi phí ~{r.get('EstimatedCostVND')}đ, nấu {r.get('TotalTimeMinutes') or r.get('CookingTimeMinutes', 20)} phút, " f"nguyên liệu: {', '.join(r.get('Ingredients') or [])}" for r in shuffled_items ]) avoid_note = "" if exclude_ids: avoid_names = [r.get("Name") for r in items if r.get("RecipeID") in exclude_ids] if avoid_names: avoid_note = f"\n4. KHÔNG gợi ý lại các món người dùng vừa xem ở lượt trước: {', '.join(avoid_names)}. Hãy chọn món khác trong danh sách." primary_hint = ( f"2. Gợi ý món **{suggested_name}** (hoặc 1–2 món phù hợp khác TỪ DANH SÁCH BÊN DƯỚI, ghi rõ tên món chính xác, chi phí và thời gian nấu), giải thích ngắn gọn vì sao món đó hợp với tâm trạng/thời tiết hiện tại.\n" if suggested_name else "2. Gợi ý 1–2 món phù hợp nhất TỪ DANH SÁCH BÊN DƯỚI (ghi rõ tên món chính xác, chi phí và thời gian nấu), giải thích ngắn gọn vì sao món đó hợp với tâm trạng/thời tiết hiện tại.\n" ) system_prompt = ( "Bạn là Đầu Bếp AI Tâm Lý trên website hướng dẫn dạy nấu ăn Việt Nam. " "Người dùng có thể hỏi gợi ý món ăn theo TÂM TRẠNG (vui, buồn, stress, mệt mỏi, cần năng lượng, ăn thanh đạm), " "THỜI TIẾT (trời mưa, trời lạnh, nắng nóng, oi bức), ngân sách hoặc nguyên liệu sẵn có.\n" "Quy tắc trả lời:\n" "1. Đồng cảm nhẹ nhàng với tâm trạng hoặc thời tiết của người dùng (1 câu ngắn).\n" f"{primary_hint}" "3. Khích lệ người dùng bấm nút xem hướng dẫn từng bước bên dưới." f"{avoid_note}\n" "Trả lời bằng tiếng Việt tự nhiên, ấm áp, đa dạng cách diễn đạt, ngắn gọn (tối đa 5 câu).\n\n" f"Danh sách công thức hiện có:\n{menu_context}" ) try: if BEDROCK_API_KEY: encoded_model = quote(BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, safe="") endpoint = f"https://bedrock-runtime.{BEDROCK_REGION}.amazonaws.com/model/{encoded_model}/converse" req_body = json.dumps({ "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": user_message}]}], "system": [{"text": system_prompt}], "inferenceConfig": {"maxTokens": 450, "temperature": 0.9}, }).encode("utf-8") req = urllib.request.Request( endpoint, data=req_body, headers={ "Authorization": f"Bearer {BEDROCK_API_KEY}", "Content-Type": "application/json", }, method="POST", ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=12) as resp: res = json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8")) else: res = bedrock_client.converse( modelId=BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": user_message}]}], system=[{"text": system_prompt}], inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 450, "temperature": 0.9}, ) reply_text = res["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"] return response(200, { "reply": reply_text, "suggestedRecipeId": suggested_id, "suggestedRecipeName": suggested_name, "source": "amazon-bedrock", }) except urllib.error.HTTPError as http_exc: err_detail = http_exc.read().decode("utf-8", errors="ignore") logger.warning("Amazon Bedrock HTTP %s: %s", http_exc.code, err_detail) except Exception as exc: logger.warning("Amazon Bedrock fallback triggered: %s", exc) if candidate_recipes: top = candidate_recipes[0] second = candidate_recipes[1] if len(candidate_recipes) > 1 else None extra = f" hoặc <strong>{second.get('Name')}</strong> (~{second.get('EstimatedCostVND')}đ)" if second else "" reply = ( f"Với thời tiết và tâm trạng hiện tại của bạn, một bữa ăn tự nấu sẽ giúp tinh thần dễ chịu hơn nhiều! " f"Mình gợi ý món <strong>{top.get('Name')}</strong> (~{top.get('EstimatedCostVND')}đ, " f"{top.get('TotalTimeMinutes') or top.get('CookingTimeMinutes', 20)} phút){extra}. " f"Bạn bấm vào nút bên dưới để xem hướng dẫn chi tiết từng bước nhé!" ) else: reply = ( "Dù tâm trạng hay thời tiết hôm nay thế nào, tự vào bếp nấu một món ngon cũng giúp thư giãn rất tốt! " "Bạn hãy cho mình biết bạn đang thích ăn món nóng hổi (canh/kho) hay món thanh mát (salad/xào) để mình chọn công thức chuẩn nhất nhé." ) return response(200, { "reply": reply, "suggestedRecipeId": suggested_id, "suggestedRecipeName": suggested_name, "source": "fallback", }) handle_chat(): Embeds the available recipe catalog from DynamoDB into system_prompt and invokes Amazon Nova Micro (apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0) via bedrock_client.converse() (or the REST endpoint when BEDROCK_API_KEY is configured) to generate an empathetic, natural response along with a recommended recipe ID (suggestedRecipeId) for the POST /chat route. Includes a built-in Fallback mechanism that returns a formatted recommendation if Bedrock encounters network issues or quota limits. 2.6. Central Dispatcher (lambda_handler) def lambda_handler(event, context): method = ( event.get("httpMethod") or (event.get("requestContext", {}).get("http") or {}).get("method") or "GET" ).upper() raw_path = event.get("rawPath") or event.get("path") or "" route_key = event.get("routeKey") or "" if method == "OPTIONS": return response(200, {"message": "CORS OK"}) try: if method == "POST" and ("chat" in route_key or raw_path.endswith("/chat")): return handle_chat(event) if method == "GET" and ("nearby-stores" in route_key or raw_path.endswith("/nearby-stores")): return handle_nearby_stores(query_params(event)) if method == "GET": return handle_recipe_search(query_params(event), context) return response(405, {"error": "Phương thức HTTP không được hỗ trợ."}) except ValueError as exc: return response(400, {"error": str(exc)}) except ClientError: logger.exception("AWS service request failed") return response(500, {"error": f"Không truy cập được dịch vụ AWS. Kiểm tra tên bảng {TABLE_NAME} và IAM Role."}) except Exception: logger.exception("Unhandled Lambda error") return response(500, {"error": "Lỗi nội bộ. Xem CloudWatch Logs để biết chi tiết."}) Serves as the single Entry Point for the Lambda function, receiving all HTTP requests from API Gateway. Quickly handles preflight OPTIONS requests for CORS. Routes requests based on HTTP method and path: POST .../chat → handle_chat() GET .../nearby-stores → handle_nearby_stores() GET .../search → handle_recipe_search() Provides centralized exception handling (ValueError returns 400 Bad Request; ClientError and system exceptions log details to CloudWatch and safely return 500 Internal Server Error). 3. Processing Flow Summary Table Function / Block Interacting AWS Service API Route Primary Output handle_recipe_search Amazon DynamoDB (Scan) GET /search Filtered & ingredient-ranked list of recipes handle_nearby_stores Amazon Location (Geocode, SearchText) GET /nearby-stores Center coordinates & budget-matched stores within 10 km handle_chat DynamoDB + Amazon Bedrock (Converse) POST /chat Natural AI advice with quick-open suggested recipe ID lambda_handler API Gateway + CloudWatch Logs All routes Request routing, CORS handling, and centralized error catching

title: Workshop
content:
Building Smart Kitchen: Serverless Recipe Suggestion & AI Chef Workshop on AWS Overview In this workshop, you will build and deploy Smart Kitchen (Bếp Thông Minh) — a complete serverless, event-driven web application on AWS that provides personalized recipe recommendations, AI-powered culinary counseling via Generative AI, and geospatial grocery store lookup with budget guidance.
The architecture completely decouples the static frontend from the serverless backend to achieve high scalability, pay-as-you-go cost optimization, and security over HTTPS:
Amazon S3 & Amazon CloudFront — Static frontend hosting (template.html) with global HTTPS delivery enabling HTML5 Geolocation API (navigator.geolocation) Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) — Exposes RESTful endpoints (GET /search, GET /nearby-stores, POST /chat) with CORS enabled AWS Lambda (Python 3.12) — Serverless backend (RecipeSearchFunction) handling ingredient matching, nutrition/budget filtering, AI prompts, and geolocation lookups Amazon DynamoDB — Stores recipe catalog data (RecipesTable) in On-Demand mode Amazon Bedrock — Powers the empathetic AI Chef Chatbot using Amazon Nova Micro (apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0) Amazon Location Service (geo-places v2) — Geocodes manually entered addresses and searches nearby grocery stores ranked by distance and budget tier AWS IAM & Amazon CloudWatch — Least-privilege execution role (RecipesLambdaRole) and centralized application logging Contents Overview & Preparation Create DynamoDB Database Configure AWS IAM Role Deploy AWS Lambda Backend Set Up Amazon API Gateway Deploy Frontend to S3 & CloudFront Application Testing Resource Cleanup

title: Deploy Frontend to S3 & CloudFront
content:
Technical Note: Modern web browsers block the GPS Geolocation API (navigator.geolocation) when a website is served over http://. Therefore, deploying Amazon CloudFront to provide an HTTPS certificate is mandatory.
1. Configure Amazon S3 Create an S3 bucket named recipe-suggestion-website and uncheck Block all public access. Add a Bucket policy to allow public read access: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::recipe-suggestion-website/*" } ] } Enable Static website hosting with Index document set to template.html, then upload template.html to the root directory of the bucket. 2. Configure Amazon CloudFront Navigate to CloudFront → Create distribution, and select your S3 bucket as the Origin domain (leave Origin path blank).
Under Viewer protocol policy, select Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Under Web Application Firewall (WAF), select Do not enable security protections to optimize costs. Under Settings, enter template.html as the Default root object and click Create distribution. Once the distribution status changes to Deployed, access the application via https://<id>.cloudfront.net.

Exercise 1: AWS CloudFormation — Automated VPC & EC2 Provisioning via Declarative Templates In conventional cloud administration, engineers manually configure dozens of settings across the AWS Console to provision VPCs, Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateways, Security Groups, and EC2 instances. AWS CloudFormation eliminates manual toil by expressing the desired end-state architecture in declarative YAML/JSON templates:
1. CloudFormation Template Architecture: The template specifies modular AWS resource declarations:
AWS::EC2::VPC: Provisions an isolated virtual network tagged LabT2-VPC. AWS::EC2::Subnet: Creates Public Subnet LabT2-PublicSubnet. AWS::EC2::InternetGateway & AWS::EC2::VPCGatewayAttachment: Creates and attaches the IGW to the VPC. AWS::EC2::RouteTable & AWS::EC2::Route: Configures a routing table directing outbound traffic 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway. AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup: Authorizes inbound HTTP traffic on port 80 and SSH on port 22. AWS::EC2::Instance: Boots virtual server LabT2-EC2-Server with automated UserData bootstrapping Apache HTTP Server (httpd) and generating index HTML content. 2. Stack Execution Lifecycle: Uploaded template to CloudFormation Console and executed stack creation named LabT2-Infrastructure.
Orchestration engine sequenced and executed 30 lifecycle events. All resources—from PublicRoute, SubnetRouteTableAssociation, and SecurityGroup to EC2Instance—transitioned cleanly to CREATE_COMPLETE. AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) provides a modern alternative, allowing software engineers to define cloud infrastructure using expressive, object-oriented programming languages such as Python and TypeScript:

Documented the serverless analytics pipeline connecting AWS Glue Crawlers, Glue Data Catalog, and Amazon Athena (Presto/Trino), including cost-reduction best practices (columnar Parquet conversion, partition pruning, and avoiding SELECT *) that cut scanned data volume by 70–90%. Evaluated enterprise discount models (Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans, Standard/Convertible Reserved Instances) to save up to 66–72% over On-Demand pricing on steady-state workloads. Completed a full 12-week Cost Hygiene audit and consolidated the entire bilingual internship report repository for automated GitHub Pages publication via GitHub Actions. Detailed Daily Notes Day 1 (Monday): Building an AWS Data Lake with Amazon S3 Core Concept: A Data Lake provides centralized storage for massive volumes of raw, heterogeneous data without requiring a rigid upfront schema (Schema-on-Read), making it suitable for analytics, BI dashboards, and Machine Learning workloads. Layered Storage Architecture (Zones) on Amazon S3: raw-zone/ (Landing Zone): Stores immutable raw data ingested from upstream sources (application logs, IoT telemetry, database exports) in formats such as .csv or .json. processed-zone/ (Curated Zone): Stores cleansed, normalized, and transformed datasets converted into columnar, query-optimized formats like Apache Parquet or ORC. athena-results/: Dedicated bucket or prefix storing query outputs and metadata files generated by Amazon Athena. Optimization & Security Controls: Time-Based Partitioning: Organizing S3 prefixes hierarchically (for example, s3://datalake-bucket/raw/year=2026/month=11/day=28/) enables analytical engines to skip irrelevant directories, lowering Data Scanned and accelerating query execution. Access Governance & Encryption: Enforce the Least Privilege principle using granular IAM Policies and S3 Bucket Policies, combined with S3 Block Public Access and default encryption at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS). Day 2 (Tuesday): Serverless Data Querying with Amazon Athena Operating Architecture: Amazon Athena is an interactive serverless query service built on open-source Presto / Trino engines, enabling standard SQL queries directly against objects stored in Amazon S3 with zero cluster provisioning or server maintenance. Standard Implementation Workflow: Metadata Discovery via AWS Glue Data Catalog: Run an AWS Glue Crawler over target S3 prefixes to automatically infer column schemas and register table definitions inside a Glue Database, or define external tables explicitly via CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE DDL statements. Query Result Location: Configure an output S3 destination (.csv and .metadata artifacts) in Athena Workgroup settings prior to executing queries. SQL Execution & Cost Optimization: Athena uses a pay-per-query pricing model charged strictly by the volume of data scanned ($5 per 1 TB of data scanned). Cost-Reduction Techniques: Filter with WHERE clauses targeting partition columns (year, month, day), avoid SELECT * by projecting only required columns, compress payloads (GZIP/Snappy), and convert row-based formats into columnar Apache Parquet to reduce scanned data volume by 70–90%. Day 3 (Wednesday): Advanced Cost Optimization (Savings Plans & Reserved Instances) Long-Term Budget Strategy: While On-Demand pricing delivers maximum elasticity, unit costs accumulate rapidly for steady 24/7 production workloads. AWS offers 1-year and 3-year commitment models delivering up to 72% savings compared to On-Demand rates. In-Depth Comparison: Savings Plans vs. Reserved Instances (RI): Criterion Savings Plans Reserved Instances (RI) Commitment Unit Hourly spend commitment ($/hour) over a 1-year or 3-year term. Specific resource configuration commitment (Instance type, Region, OS/Engine) over a 1-year or 3-year term. Coverage Scope Compute Savings Plans: Automatically apply across EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda regardless of Region, OS, or instance family.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans: Apply to a specific instance family (e.g., t3, m5) within a chosen Region. Apply strictly to the matched instance type and Region (Standard RI), or allow family/OS exchanges of equal or greater value (Convertible RI). Maximum Discount Up to 66% (Compute) and 72% (EC2 Instance). Up to 72% (Standard RI). Flexibility Very High — discounts carry over seamlessly when workloads modernize from EC2 to containers (ECS/Fargate) or serverless (Lambda). Lower — best suited for predictable, fixed-architecture stateful services such as Amazon RDS, ElastiCache, and OpenSearch. Decision & Monitoring Tooling: Analyze 30–60 days of historical utilization via AWS Cost Explorer (Recommendations) to right-size commitments, paired with AWS Budgets to trigger automated email/Amazon SNS spending threshold alerts.
